To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the abundance and diversity of insect herbivore species were 2.3 and 2.5 times higher, respectively, on mature trees than on sapling hosts of a common tropical tree, and that the abundance of young foliage was the main driver of these differences.

insect herbivores are more abundant and diverse on the foliage of canopy trees than on that of sapling trees of Pouroumma bicolor, and that host stage and young foliage are important factors in explaining the spatial distributions of herbivore assemblages in a tropical forest canopy.

(i) herbivore abundance and richness are higher on trees than saplings; (ii) the difference is due to the higher availability of young foliage on trees; (iii) the difference may be partly due to other factors, such as resource quality or enemy-free space; and (iv) the differences between host stages may be underestimated because of pseudo-replication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distribution of insect herbivore communities between saplings and trees in a wet forest in Panama.
the spatial distribution of insect herbivore populations on a tropical tree, and the factors influencing this distribution.
the effects of host stage on herbivore abundance and species richness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
insect herbivores are more abundant and diverse in the upper canopy of a tropical wet forest than at the base of the forest.
the canopy is a more complex and diverse habitat for insect herbivores than the understorey.
the sapling stage of P. bicolour supports a less abundant and species-poor herbivore community than the mature tree stage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the abundance and richness of insect herbives are higher on mature trees than on sapling trees in a tropical wet rainforest in Panama.
herbivores are more abundant on mature trees than on sapling hosts.
herbivores were more abundant and species rich on the foliage of mature trees than on that of sapplings of P. bicolour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
insect herbivore communities in tropical forests are not static, and the composition and abundance of insect herbivore species can change dramatically as trees grow and mature.
the canopy is an important habitat for many species, including insect herbivores, that are not present on the ground or in the understory.

the abundance and species richness, but not the composition, of herbivore communities feeding on a given plant species is strongly influenced by the host plant stage, and that this influence is likely to be greater in tropical forests than in temperate ones.
